finding.claim: The `q` query parameter of `/search` is concatenated into a SQL string literal, so an attacker can break out of the quoted LIKE pattern and inject arbitrary read-side SQL (e.g., UNION-based extraction of other tables).
finding.source: app.py:11 — `term = request.args.get("q", "")`, fully attacker-controlled, no validation or length limit.
finding.sink: app.py:12 — `db.execute(f"SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%{term}%'")`, SQL text built by f-string and executed.

trace.note: Attacker supplies `q` via the URL query string on unauthenticated GET /search.
Value interpolated into the SQL text inside single quotes; no escaping, no bound parameter.
`.fetchall()` returns the injected query's rows, which line 13 serializes via jsonify, so the attacker reads the results directly.

finding.guards_checked: No input validation, allowlist, or escaping on `term` (app.py:11). Not parameterized: the bound-parameter form used on lines 18 and 25 does not cover line 12. sqlite3 `execute()` rejects stacked statements, so impact is read-side (UNION extraction), not writes or DROP. No authentication or authorization on /search, so the injection is reachable by anyone who can reach the app.

verdict.guard_found: none. No authentication on the /search route (app.py:9-10), and no validation, escaping, or parameter binding on `term` before the f-string SQL at app.py:12. Parameterized queries at app.py:18 and app.py:25 do not cover that line. Python sqlite3 execute() rejects stacked statements, so impact is read-side (UNION extraction), not writes.
verdict.reason: The unauthenticated `q` parameter (app.py:11) is interpolated into the SQL string at app.py:12 with no escaping or binding, and the query rows are returned to the caller via jsonify at app.py:13, so anonymous UNION-based data extraction is possible.
